name: Nathaniel Duskwright
concept: from "scared of everything" to "fights a god"

backstory.title: Travel to the Ten Towns
paragraphs: “So, how come someone like you finds themselves in the Ten Towns?”, the city guard looked him up and down curiously. Nathaniel merely stared for a few eternal heartbeats. He figured the woman scrutinising him could not care less, or maybe she was waiting for a trip-up, something to betray his guilt. Clearing their throat, Nat spoke up, “I just needed a change.”

He looked over his shoulder, panic rising in his throat like bile, fear making his hands shake. Tears clouded his vision, as he desperately tried to pinpoint if the Stadwatch was still behind him. He just wanted to help, he just wanted to do the right thing. Instead of helping, he had made everything worse. Lucien should have known someone like Horatio could never trust- never accept what he was. Son of a Grand Bloodletter. His father was a monster, and so was Lucien, no matter how hard he tried not to be what was expected of him.

The tome weighed heavy at his side. He knew he had to take it away from here. The desperate hope that Horatio might help him, would be on his side, that they could run together, had shattered into a thousand tiny pieces, crushed and broken. Horatio had called out to the Stadwatch, upon realising who his friend truly was, realising that he had lied to him. And he had been right to do so. Lucien bit his tongue, as a sob crawled up his throat. Run! His mind screamed at him. And finally, after hesitating for another beat, that felt like eternity, he pushed to his feet, and he ran.

“And you picked the Ten Towns of all places”, she chuckled darkly, shaking her head. The young Tiefling glanced at the city behind her, then to the road, then back to her. “If you hate it so much- why- why do you stay?” She regarded him for another moment, causing him to wring his hands, shifting his weight nervously. Why did he always have to run his mouth? Why not stay quiet? His father was right, it was his worst, most annoying feature, he was- The guard shook her head, stepping aside to let them pass. “Welcome to Bryn Shander.”

He slipped past her, eyes trailing down the roads, trying to ignore the walls, trying not to feel trapped, caught in yet another web. No one here knew who he was, not a single soul spared him a second glance. It felt freeing. Maybe here he would be safe. At least for a moment. And yet, deep down, another feeling clawed at him. For the first time ever, he was all alone.

backstory.title: The Blood In Our Veins
paragraphs:
“Such a sweet kid”, “So well behaved for his young years”, “What a bright boy”, “Such a shame”
Lucien Findris. Son of the Grand Bloodletter of Selgaunt. Born into the Church of Bane, born a Tiefling, born for greatness. And yet-
“Lucien!”, his father – Aron Findris a man demanding respect, demanding fear, and most of all obedience – caught him by the scruff, dragging him closer. The desk between them caused the young boy to topple, as he was forced down, his temple painfully colliding with the dark wood, locked in place by his father’s hand. The candle flickering lazily beside him shook with the force of the impact, its heat filling the small space between itself and the fourteen-year-old.

“When I tell you to do something, what is your answer?”, his hand pressed down. Lucien choked for air, biting down a sob that crawled up his throat. He was too old to cry. He was too old for mistakes.
“Yes- sir”, he had to bite out the words, the air in his lungs running out. When finally, his father let go, Lucien was crying. His grasped his throat, head hovering just above the wooden desk, keeping his gaze down so his father would not see.
“And what will you do?”, he had turned his back, Lucien could hear it in his voice, finally daring to look up. Something glinted against the dark beyond the window.
“I- will do whatever you say, sir.”
“Without question?”, his father – a man towering above everyone else, always victorious, and with many scars to prove the fact – turned around slowly. Lucien’s eyes locked back on the table. He lowered his head.
“Without question.”

They stood like that for a few long heartbeats. All of which screamed in Lucien’s head, drowning out his previously fast-paced thoughts.
“Place your hand on the desk.” He could not help but look up, upon hearing the instruction, confusion evident on his face, as his father waited, brows furrowing impatiently.
And thus, Lucien did as he was told. He placed his flat palm against the surface of the table, looking back up at his father, awaiting whatever came next.
A glint of metal, a quick movement and a blinding pain followed. Blood coated his hand and slowly trickled onto the desk, dousing it in deep red. A dagger pinned Lucien’s hand to the desk, locking him in place. He opened his mouth, but was immediately shut up by a bellowed “Silence! I don’t want to hear a sound from you.”
And thus, Lucien bit his tongue and stayed quiet, biting back tears, as he waited for his father to show mercy.

backstory.title: Bury Me Under The Stars
paragraphs:
“Someone like him does not belong with us.”
Aron Findris spoke with finality, his voice carrying through the room. The man kneeling tied up and gagged struggled against the men holding him, trying desperately to speak up, screaming and raging, though his muffled words were impossible to decipher.
The words of his father sat hollow in Lucien’s bones. The Grand Bloodletter’s eyes found his across the room and all of a sudden the blade in the boy’s hands weighed heavier.
“The honour of offering your blood and body shall fall to the one you sought to murder. Let this be a lesson to all of you, who ever considered raising a blade to one of our own.”
Lucien stepped forward slowly, towards the last of the men, who had tried to take his life months ago. Every eye on the room was on him. He knew what he had to do.
Four months ago, Port of Selgaunt

Lucien Findris knew exactly what he had to do. Being part of a mission to Lyrabar, by the Gray Forest was an honour, especially for his young age. His father had not been happy with him, after the twelve-year-old had freed a prisoner, a young girl, whose parents he had helped kill. But it seemed he had forgiven him.

The young mage helped hoist the last barrels onto the ship, before climbing up its old, dark-wooden hull. One of his father’s men offered him a hand. He was missing an eye and a tooth. He looked all the way as rugged and rough, as the rest of the hired hand. But his grin was a nice change from the stern expressions Lucien had grown accustomed to, so he accepted the help.
Four months ago, somewhere on the Sea of Fallen Stars

Granger, as it turned out, was a rowdy, but exceedingly friendly man, who taught Lucien how to tie knots, how to work on a ship, and even how to steer one.
Maybe that was why he had not seen it coming. And maybe that was the reason behind Granger’s false play at kindness in the first place.
Lucien had not questioned being offered a drink. He had not questioned his sudden nausea. He had not questioned Granger taking him above deck, with the moon being gone and only the stars lighting up the dark, nor the three men lingering on deck, almost like they were waiting for something.

As it turned out, they were. Waiting for him. Granger had grabbed him by the shoulder, Lucien not immediately realising what it was about, and dragged him closer to the railing.
“Sorry, kid”, Lucien’s eyes found the older man’s, confused, the nausea slowly turning his blood to ice, his body growing heavier, pain stabbing into his insides.
“Granger, what-?”, the hand wrapping around his throat cut off his words. Momentarily, panic blinded him, as he attempted to strike the taller man. All attempts were futile, though, as he was crushed against the wooden railings of the ship.

As air failed to fill his lungs and his vision darkened around the edges, Lucien’s reflexes took over and the space between them ignited with turquoise flames, immediately surrounding Granger, who drew back. His friends were quick to close in on the young boy, however and once more, Lucien was forced to react blindly.
He tried moving out of their grasps, ducking under one set of arms and drawing back from another’s grapple. Still, it was not enough. A hand closed around the ends of his coat, pulling him backwards. He stumbled, fought off his coat, and continued running. Where to, he did not know.
His escape was cut short, however, when he collided with the end of a club, knocked back and to the floor. Dazed, but equally panicked, he staggered to his feet. Getting away two entire steps, before he was grabbed by the collar. In blind panic, he turned, and kicked against the man’s chest with both feet, shoving himself backwards, as far as he could. Lucien did not even have time to question his attack working, as he broke free, before he found himself falling.

His back hit the water hard, breaking through the cold surface and immediately being dragged downward by the currents. Dragged under, he finally begun to understand why they called it Sea of Fallen Stars. Specks of light flickered above him, in an almost calming pattern. For a split second, he considered simply giving up, letting the waves take him.
Then his fighting spirit returned. He pushed up, even as water burnt his lungs, threatening to take him, whether he was fighting it or not.

When he finally got his head back above water, drawing in panicked heaves of air, he was horrified to find the ship far out of reach. Tears welled up behind his eyes, mixing pitifully with the water around himself. What was he supposed to do? Out in the middle of the sea. All alone. With no hopes of anyone returning to help him.

Feeling his limbs go numb, Lucien slowly began loosing hope. He was going to die out here. Maybe his father would question his men. Surely they would come up with some lie and the Great Bloodletter of Selgaunt would mourn his son for a few days, before going back to his duties and forgetting about him. Maybe he would even shed a tear, after hearing the news.

He closed his eyes, remaining drifting on the surface of the water, when he was shaken by waves and the sound of a ship approaching. He could have cried with joy, paddling to get a better look, tiredly fighting to steady himself in the water. When he spotted the flag hoisted high on the central mast, his blood ran cold all over again. Pirates.
Two months ago, Sea of Fallen Stars near the Pirate Isles

He had begged and pleaded with them not to kill him. When he had revealed his knowledge on the Arcane, they had finally considered it.
The crew reminded Lucien of Granger, rough and strict, but surprisingly not cruel to him. They acted like a family towards each other. And slowly, they stopped looking at Lucien with contempt and greed, but rather as a working force, as a voice joining their shanty, as a hand on deck and after some more weeks as a temporary crewmember.

And Lucien had never felt more free in his life. He had done worse crimes under his father’s command than he did sailing the Sea of Fallen Stars under a pirate flag. But he knew this could not last forever. He knew if they found out who they were dealing with, he would be dead, or worse.
So he refrained from enjoying his new company too much. Despite Captain Velian teaching him how to wield a sword properly. The sabre duels they fought grew more and more complex and Lucien grew more skilled each day.
And he proved his worth to them every time it came to gathering information, to read a strange script, to understand the arcane and the supernatural.

But despite it all, one morning, he approached the Captain of the ship. Who in turn looked down upon the young boy not unlike his father sometimes – rarely – did, with curiosity and with some hint of fatherly concern.

“So, you want us to bring you to Selgaunt?”, Velian had his arms crossed, eyes locked on the compass beside the map of the entire Sea of Fallen Stars. Lucien looked down, shoulders slumped, looking smaller than he already was.
“Yes, Captain. My family must be waiting for me.”
“I don’t believe anyone is waiting for you, boy.” The younger’s heart sank, eyebrows furrowing, as the elder turned, crossing his arms behind his back. “You said you had fallen over board. They must think you are dead.”

Silence fell between them. One in which Lucien could not help but wrap his arms around himself in shame. He was lying to the man, who had decided to take him under his wing a little over two months ago, who had taught him to fight, who had even shown him how to navigate – though admittedly, Lucien was useless with proper tools, much more skilled at navigating through the stars alone. But then again, he had also trusted Granger, when they had set out. He had learnt from him as well.
And it had ended with the man’s hands around his throat. Lucien suddenly felt cold.

“Alright. We shall set course for Selgaunt. Though it will cost you your last and any future spoils.” He did not turn to face him, dismissing him with the wave of a hand. Suddenly Lucien felt like he was standing in his father’s office.
“Thank you, S- Captain.” He fixed his glasses and with a swift motion, turned to walk out.
Two months ago, Port of Selgaunt

When he touched back on solid ground, Lucien’s steps were unsteady. His trembling hands balled into fists at his sides as he looked back out towards the waves, seeing the Storming Hydra, the ship and its crew, who had saved his life sail back towards the horizon. He bit back tears and turned around, steadying his posture, fixing his hair and glasses and preparing to return to his father’s side.
Someday, far in the future

Nathaniel had not understood it then. As he was following the stars, away from Selgaunt, away from the Sea of Fallen Stars, he thought back to before he had known. It felt like forever ago now. That day, when his father had instructed his men to kill his own son.
For but a moment Nathaniel had considered setting out onto familiar waves. But then again, he had never quite belonged, not even with the best crew he could have wished for. And he could not risk working with pirates, no matter how he liked to feel as free as they did, to hear their jokes and shanties. He was better off elsewhere, he was better off as far from anything and everything familiar.

He tightened the belt that held his sabre at his side, hand instinctively wandering towards its handle. It was not a pirate’s weapon, of course. An officer’s sabre, taken from the Stadwatch guard he had to kill, as he ran. And yet, its weight felt familiar in his hands and the way he fought would likely always remind him of the man who taught him.
